name: Bonapartism

keyFigures.role: Napoleon III, who used his uncle's legacy to build the Second Empire and wrote Des idées napoléoniennes.
keyFigures.quote: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte ( Napoleon III , 1808–1873) used to construct and destroy a Second Empire

summary: Bonapartism is rule by a charismatic leader who claims to embody the people's will, combining a strong centralised state, army and bureaucracy with plebiscitary legitimacy. It promises to end revolutionary disorder and class conflict, reconcile authority with popular rights and 1789 equality, and deliver national glory and material progress through state-led growth, while suppressing organised opposition.
scope: The Napoleonic idea as set out by Louis-Napoléon in Des idées napoléoniennes (1839) and the 1852 constitution, and as practised in the Second Empire (1852-1870), with Napoleon I's tradition behind it. Excludes Marx's critical use of the word, the broad modern sense for any military strongman, and later neo-Bonapartist strands.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Louis-Napoléon praises the Banque de France as part of the admirable financial system still in force.

class-collaboration.rationale: As emperor he set up societies of mutual assistance and boards of arbitration so that employers and employees would understand each other.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The text says the ruling idea of Napoleon was not war but a social, industrial, commercial and humane idea.

conscription.rationale: Louis-Napoléon calls the conscription 'one of the greatest institutions of the age' because it consecrated equality and defended independence.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Larousse says Bonapartist power rests on heredity but also on a delegation from the nation as the principle of all sovereignty; Britannica calls it autocratic government with the people's consent.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The constitution was written by the president himself under powers delegated by plebiscite, after he dissolved the elected Legislative Assembly.

decide-locally.rationale: The president appoints to all posts (art. 6), which gives a centralised administration under his authority.

direct-votes.rationale: The constitution and the empire were both put to plebiscite, and art. 32 submits any change to its fundamental bases to universal suffrage; ordinary laws were not.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Art. 12 lets the president declare a state of siege in any département, reporting to the Senate afterwards.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Art. 1 guarantees the 1789 principles, art. 26 lets the Senate block laws against them, and art. 32 requires a plebiscite to change the fundamental bases.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Art. 1 confirms the 1789 principles and art. 26 has the Senate block laws against the equality of citizens before the law.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Napoleon III took the initiative in foreign affairs from the start and intervened in Italy, Rome, Lebanon and Mexico.

free-trade.rationale: The 1860 commercial treaty with Britain began a free-trade policy aimed at higher prosperity and lower living costs, and customs barriers were lowered.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Art. 6 gives the president command of land and sea forces and the power to declare war.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: The text holds that the human race advances constantly toward perfection.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The text calls the Napoleonic idea a social, industrial, commercial and humane one.

leader-cult.rationale: Larousse lists personalisation of executive power among Bonapartism's fundamental principles, and the Napoleonic text calls the Emperor the Messiah of modern ideas.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The constitution sets a Senate of notables (cardinals, marshals, admirals, appointees) beside a Corps législatif elected by universal suffrage, under a hereditary-style executive.

national-self-determination.rationale: Napoleon III fought Austria to free Italians and made the principle of nationality his stated aim, but did not dare to support Poland in 1863.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The text rejects calling government a necessary ulcer: it is the beneficent power that imparts motion to all social organisation.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Larousse says Napoleon III's regime wanted to stand above parties.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The president alone initiates laws, amendments pass through the Council of State and he convenes and dissolves the Corps législatif (arts. 8, 40, 46).

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The 2 December 1851 coup was carried through by force, with street fighting in Paris and arrests and deportations numbering thousands.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Art. 7 has justice rendered in the president's name; state courts stay.

property-fundamental.rationale: Art. 26 has the Senate block any law that violates the inviolability of property, alongside the constitution and individual liberty.

proportional-representation.rationale: Art. 36 elects deputies by universal suffrage 'sans scrutin de liste', one candidate at a time.

restore-past-order.rationale: The text says an attempt to bring back the ancient system would have been folly and that society's amelioration moves onward without limit.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He calls himself an enemy to every absolute theory and prefers the precepts of experience to abstract doctrines.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Louis-Napoléon holds up the constitution as leaving other means of salvation than the disastrous expedient of revolutions.

separate-church-state.rationale: Cardinals sit in the Senate by right and the Senate blocks laws against religion (arts. 20, 26); the Concordat stayed in force.

separated-powers.rationale: The constitution names a Senate, Corps législatif and Council of State (arts. 3, 4, 25-26, 39), but the president appoints them, alone initiates laws and can dissolve the Corps législatif (arts. 8, 46).

single-common-good.rationale: Louis-Napoléon presents the Council of State and one-way legislation as ending the sterile agitation and passionate struggles of parliamentary politics.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Napoleon III promoted public works, railways and credit institutions, and took the initiative in everything useful for prosperity.

state-harmful.rationale: The text calls government a beneficent power giving motion to social organisation, not a necessary ulcer.

strong-leader.rationale: The 1852 constitution makes the president head of state with sole initiative of laws and ministers answerable only to him (arts. 6, 8, 13); Britannica records that he ruled authoritatively.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In 1860 the Empire signed the Anglo-French commercial treaty, a new economic policy on free-trade principles.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Empire gained Nice and Savoy and extended French power in Indochina and West Africa, and sought compensation in Belgium.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Louis-Napoléon points to the Code Napoléon governing citizens' dealings and to the end of separate religious jurisdictions as foundations of the Napoleonic order.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Louis-Napoléon, barred from re-election by the constitution, carried out the 2 December 1851 coup and took ten-year then imperial office.

notes: Themes searched: government, liberty, world, economy, society, means. Answers rest on Larousse, Britannica, the 1852 constitution and proclamation, and Des idées napoléoniennes; Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire is a critic's text and answers nothing.
